title: Modern C++ Essentials
relevance: Modern C++ features (auto, lambdas, smart pointers, brace init) are expected in SDE interviews as the baseline for writing safer, idiomatic C++.

phases.goal: Establish what core modern C++ features exist and what problem each solves.

must_hit.point: auto deduces a variable's type from its initializer and by default strips references and const, producing an independent copy.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says auto drops & and const unless you write auto& or const auto&.

must_hit.point: nullptr is a type-safe null pointer constant that converts to any pointer type but never to an integer, unlike NULL/0 which caused overload ambiguity.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts print(NULL) often calling print(int) with print(nullptr) unambiguously calling the pointer overload.

must_hit.point: A lambda is an anonymous inline function object with syntax [captures](parameters) -> return_type { body }; the compiler creates a unique unnamed closure type with operator() and members for captures.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Defines closure as the generated function object and notes each lambda expression has a distinct type.

must_hit.point: Smart pointers in <memory> codify RAII: unique_ptr is exclusive ownership, shared_ptr is shared ownership via a reference count, weak_ptr observes without owning.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States prefer smart pointers over raw new/delete and can sketch the three ownership roles.

must_hit.point: Uniform brace initialization prevents narrowing conversions that parentheses/equals initialization allow.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives int a = 3.14 compiling vs int b{3.14} as an error.

must_hit.point: C++17 structured bindings unpack a tuple, pair, or struct into named variables in one declaration.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions for (const auto& [id, name] : users) style unpacking.

probes: What does auto deduce when assigned from a const reference, and how do you avoid the copy?
Compare unique_ptr, shared_ptr, and weak_ptr at a high level.

hints.1: Think about what auto keeps versus what it drops from the initializer.
hints.2: Cover auto/decltype basics, nullptr vs NULL, lambda closures, and the three smart-pointer ownership models.
hints.3: auto strips const and & (need const auto&); nullptr never converts to int; lambdas become unique closures; unique/shared/weak map to exclusive, counted shared, and non-owning observe.

phases.goal: Explain how deduction, captures, initialization, and ownership counting actually behave.

must_hit.point: Plain auto return deduction drops references and top-level const/volatile; decltype(auto) (C++14) applies decltype rules to the return expression and preserves references and value category.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts auto by_value() copying g with decltype(auto) by_ref() yielding std::string&.

must_hit.point: std::vector<int> v1(5, 2) uses the size/value constructor producing five 2s; v2{5, 2} prefers the initializer_list constructor producing [5, 2].
must_hit.evidence_hint: Clearly distinguishes parentheses constructor overload from braced initializer_list.

must_hit.point: Lambda captures: [x, &y] mixed; [=] all by value; [&] all by reference; by-value captures are read-only unless the lambda is mutable, and mutable only mutates the closure's copy.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains [=]/[&]/mixed captures and that mutable does not change the original variable.

must_hit.point: In a member function, naming members captures this by pointer ([this] or [=]); [*this] (C++17) copies the object into the closure so the original can be destroyed safely.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Warns [=] does not snapshot the object and contrasts dangling [this] with [*this].

must_hit.point: Init-capture [identifier = expression] (C++14) can compute a capture, rename, or move move-only types like unique_ptr into the closure.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives [p = std::move(ptr)] or [n = x + 1] as patterns C++11 by-value capture cannot express cleanly.

must_hit.point: Only a capture-less lambda [] converts implicitly to a matching function pointer; any capture embeds state and makes that conversion ill-formed.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says a capturing closure is a class instance, not a bare code address.

must_hit.point: Prefer make_shared over constructing shared_ptr from a raw pointer because it allocates the object and reference counter in one contiguous block; weak_ptr.lock() temporarily upgrades to shared_ptr for access.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions single-block allocation/cache locality/exception safety and lock() before use.

probes: How do auto and decltype(auto) differ for deduced return types?
What can a lambda capture, and when can it convert to a function pointer?
Why is make_shared preferred, and how does weak_ptr.lock() work?

hints.1: Walk through what is preserved versus stripped, and who owns what.
hints.2: Hit return deduction, vector brace vs paren, capture rules including this/*this and init-capture, then shared_ptr counting and weak_ptr.lock().
hints.3: auto drops ref/const, decltype(auto) preserves them; (5,2) vs {5,2}; [=]/[&]/mutable/copy; [this] vs [*this]; only []→function pointer; make_shared one block; lock() to use weak_ptr.

phases.goal: Choose between closely related modern-C++ tools with clear costs and failure modes.

must_hit.point: Use auto when you intentionally want a value (copy or moved temporary); use decltype(auto) when forwarding/returning an existing object and must not strip &.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States the intentional-copy vs preserve-reference rule and notes dangling still possible if a reference to a local is deduced.

must_hit.point: Prefer unique_ptr for single ownership; shared_ptr when multiple owners must keep the object alive; weak_ptr when you need observation without extending lifetime (especially to break cycles).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Maps exclusive vs shared vs non-owning observe and names cycles as the weak_ptr motivation.

must_hit.point: Prefer explicit captures [x, &y] over default [=]/[&] in production; defaults are fine for short immediately invoked lambdas.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says explicit lists document intent and make dangling-reference review easier.

must_hit.point: Prefer auto (or a function template parameter) over std::function when you do not need one concrete type; std::function type-erases at the cost of possible heap allocation and an indirect call.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts deduced closure type efficiency with std::function's stable erased type.

probes: When would you pick decltype(auto) over auto for a return type?
When is std::function justified versus storing a lambda in auto?

hints.1: Ask what must be preserved: value, reference, ownership, or a named type.
hints.2: Compare auto vs decltype(auto), unique vs shared vs weak, explicit vs default captures, and auto vs std::function.
hints.3: auto = want a value; decltype(auto) = preserve ref/category; unique/shared/weak by ownership need; explicit captures for longevity; std::function only when type erasure is required.

phases.goal: Apply modern C++ features safely in the lifetime and initialization situations interviews probe.

must_hit.point: Prefer smart pointers over raw new and delete so RAII destroys resources when owners leave scope.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States the golden rule and describes automatic cleanup at scope exit.

must_hit.point: If two objects hold shared_ptrs to each other, reference counts never reach zero; break the cycle with weak_ptr on one side.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes the mutual shared_ptr leak and weak_ptr as the fix.

must_hit.point: A lambda stored, returned, or posted asynchronously must not hold &local, a reference into a returned stack frame, or bare [this]/[=] into an object that may die first; prefer by-value, move init-capture, or [*this].
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names dangling reference/this as a top lifetime bug and lists safer capture choices.

must_hit.point: Use an immediately invoked lambda (IIFE) to initialize a const (or constexpr) object that needs multi-statement logic you cannot write as a single expression after =.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes []{ ... }() so only the returned value lives on and const is preserved.

must_hit.point: In range-based for, prefer const auto& for reading objects without copying; use auto& when you need to modify elements in place.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists by-value copy vs const auto& preferred vs auto& for mutation.

probes: How would you safely return a lambda from a member function that must outlive the object?
Show a case where shared_ptr leaks and how weak_ptr fixes it.

hints.1: Focus on lifetimes: who owns the resource, and what does the callable still refer to later?
hints.2: Apply RAII smart pointers, cycle-breaking weak_ptr, safe lambda captures/IIFE, and range-for reference choices.
hints.3: Smart pointers over new/delete; weak_ptr breaks shared cycles; no [&]/[this] that outlive; [*this]/move capture when needed; IIFE for complex const init; const auto& in range-for.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: auto applies variable-deduction rules and drops references/top-level const—good when you want a copy. decltype(auto) deduces via decltype on the return expression and preserves lvalue/rvalue reference form for perfect return-type deduction; returning a local still dangles if the deduced type is a reference.

unique_ptr: exactly one owner, non-copyable, movable with std::move, auto-deletes at owner destruction. shared_ptr: many owners, heap reference count, destroy when last shared_ptr dies; prefer make_shared. weak_ptr: observes without owning, lock() to temporary shared_ptr, used to break shared_ptr cycles.

Explicit [x, &y] documents intent and makes dangling-reference review easier. [=]/[&] are acceptable for short immediately invoked lambdas but hide what is captured; [=] in a member function still captures this by pointer, not a deep object copy.

tradeoffs.topic: auto/template parameter vs std::function for storing callables
tradeoffs.strong_answer: auto (or a template parameter) keeps the concrete closure type with no type erasure. std::function provides a named stable signature across boundaries but may heap-allocate and call indirectly.

tradeoffs.topic: brace vs parentheses initialization for std::vector
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Parentheses select ordinary constructors (e.g. size/value). Braces often prefer initializer_list, so vector(5, 2) and vector{5, 2} mean different things.

[this] (and [=] in members) capture the object pointer and dangle if the object dies while the lambda lives. [*this] (C++17) copies the object into the closure so returning/shipping the lambda is safe relative to the original object.

gotchas.trap: Assuming auto from a const object/reference keeps const or binds a reference.
gotchas.correction: auto drops const and & and copies the base type; write const auto& (or auto&) explicitly when you need a reference.

Parenthesised id-expression makes an lvalue, so decltype(auto) deduces int& to a destroyed local—undefined behaviour. Prefer plain auto for locals unless deliberately returning a reference into a longer-lived object.

gotchas.trap: Writing std::vector<int> v{5, 2} expecting five elements with value 2.
gotchas.correction: Braces call the initializer_list constructor → [5, 2]. Use v(5, 2) for size/value construction.

gotchas.trap: Using NULL or 0 as a null pointer with overloaded print(int) and print(char*).
gotchas.correction: NULL is typically the integer 0, so the int overload is chosen. Use nullptr so only pointer overloads match.

gotchas.trap: Two objects each holding a shared_ptr to the other.
gotchas.correction: Reference counts never reach zero (leak). Make one side a weak_ptr and lock() when access is needed.

gotchas.trap: Returning or storing a lambda that captured locals with [&], or [this]/[=] into an object that is destroyed first.
gotchas.correction: Those create dangling references/this. Prefer by-value captures, init-capture with std::move, or [*this] when the callable must outlive its creator.

gotchas.trap: Assuming [=] in a member function snapshots the whole object.
gotchas.correction: [=] still captures this by pointer; member access is this->member. Use [*this] for a by-value copy of the object.

gotchas.trap: Assigning a capturing lambda to a function pointer.
gotchas.correction: Only capture-less [] lambdas convert to a matching function pointer; any capture makes the conversion ill-formed because the closure carries state.
